input.question: How allergy shots work.
input.ground_truth: They inject you with a *really tiny* amount of the allergen at first, then subsequent shots up the dosage a little bit at a time. It exposes your body to the allergen in such a way that it never freaks out and eventually realizes that there isn't actually a threat.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How allergy shots work.

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine your body has tiny guards called "immune soldiers." Sometimes, these soldiers get confused and think something harmless, like a bit of pollen from flowers, is a bad guy. That’s what happens when you have allergies—they attack the pollen and make you sneeze and itch.

Allergy shots are like giving your immune soldiers a picture of the pollen and saying, "Don’t worry, this isn’t a bad guy! See? It’s safe!"

You get a tiny, tiny bit of the thing you’re allergic to in a shot. At first, your immune soldiers might get a little worried, but every time you get the shot, they learn that it’s not really a bad guy. After many shots, your immune soldiers stop getting scared and stop causing allergy symptoms.

So, allergy shots help your body learn not to be scared of things that aren’t really dangerous!
